Thank you for your valuable feedback. We wish to address some points raised to provide further clarification and insight into our work: 

***Regarding the Eigenspace Lipschitz assumption:***  

Due to the equivalence between matrix L2 norm and spectral norm (see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_norm#Spectral_norm), the standard assumption implies the first (and most significant part of) assumption 2; assumption 2 merely gives names to the Lipschitz parameters of each eigenspace (the maximum of which is $L_H$ from the standard Hessian Lipschitz assumption due to the matrix spectral norm-L2 norm equivalence).  We show that this distinction of the per-eigenspace Lipschitz parameters from $L_H$ is important, due to the wide variance of these parameters.  See Appendix M, Theorem M.4 (introduction begins on line 1881) for a further expansion on the relation between the standard assumption and assumption 2.  Also see appendix I, in which we discuss the slow-moving property of the Hessian, which would be invalidated by assumption 2 being far from accurate.  We will highlight this point in the final version of the paper.   

We also provide 2 methods for computing these Lipschitz parameters – one inspired by ARC’s Lipschitz parameter estimation approach (Appendix J.1) (in which we restrict ourselves to only a few eigenspaces using Lanczos iterations, a common theme in optimization, e.g. [1], [2]), and the other inspired by BFGS’s Hessian estimation approach (as in algorithm AMOS).  We demonstrate throughout the paper (e.g. section 5) that these Lipschitz parameters are meaningful and align with existing optimization literature, when coupled with the theory developed in the paper. 

***Regarding the Scope of experiments:***  

We agree that the paper leans toward the theoretical side, we leave extensive experimentation to future work.  We will make an effort to include further experiments applying AMOS to additional datasets in the final version of the paper, however experiments confirming other parts of the paper range across a variety of models and datasets, confirming the theory standing behind AMOS; see for instance section 5 and appendices J and L.   

Algorithm ELMO is developed primarily as a basis on which to build our algorithm quality metric while the paper’s focus is on optimizer selection; as a result, we leave experimentation on ELMO to future work to maintain focus on the optimizer selection problem.  We do present experiments validating the conclusions stemming from this metric (see section 5), including showing that the resultant meta-algorithm (AMOS) is beneficial to training in practice.   

Since most current training works with Adam or SGD we elected to compare against these in the paper, and we selected Sophia as our state-of-the-art second-order baseline, however we’ll also make an effort to include the results of additional experiments using alternative optimizers such as K-FAC and ARC in the final version of the paper in addition to Sophia and Adam. 

***Regarding the computational overhead:***  

Due to computational constraints, we were unable to test AMOS on very large models, however we demonstrated its applicability to smaller models in the hopes that its performance will scale, and leave extensive experimentation to future work.  We will also make an effort to include the results of wall-time experiments on the final version of the paper.  In the case of Sophia, given that AMOS adds computational overhead only to the occasional iterations in which the Hessian is estimated (and reduced overhead in all other iterations), and given that the additional complexity is relatively small (AMOS requires no eigendecomposition for Sophia and performs only O(n) additional flops (specifically: computing $|\theta_t – \theta_{t-1}|$ and $\lambda^i_t – \lambda^i_{t-1}$, dividing them, and updating the Lipschitz running averages), the wall-time is expected to be small.  In particular, distributed training systems suffer from a great deal of overhead per iteration (all-reduce gradient aggregation and all-gather gradient sharing communication overhead [3], [4], as well as time for saving checkpoints to NVMe [6] and time lost to node failures (which require a restart of the system from the last checkpoint) [5]), so that such systems draw particularly strong wall-time benefits from reduced iteration count, even in scenarios where single-device systems would see a wall-time increase.  Furthermore, in limited-data scenarios it is imperative to keep the iteration count low to avoid overfitting, and the same is true in streaming/online learning scenarios where each data point may only be used once before being discarded.

summary.value: This paper studies how curvature shifts in nonconvex loss functions affect the behavior of optimization algorithms. The authors derive local upper and lower approximation models using an eigen decomposition of the hessian at the current point $\theta_t$. The prvoide a upper bound bound on a function progress using derived models. The paper also proposed two method ELMO and AMOS; ELMO uses eigen decomposistion of the hessian at the current point, while AMOS accumulate information from previous decompositions.

strengths.value:
1. The paper provide a local upper bound model using eigenvalue decomposition of the hessian matrix. This bounds can be used for both convex and non-convex functions.
2. Seems like the proposed method performs well on practice.

weaknesses.value:
1. The does not provide a thorough review and comparision with existing results on nonconvex optimzation, preconditioned method, and meta-optimizers. I believe it would be beneficial to extend the literatrure review of this paper, and make a comparison of this work in the context of previous results. I don't think that the reference provided in paper are aligned with the topic of interest of the paper. For nonconvex optimization and preconditioned method please see "Spectral Preconditioning for Gradient Methods
on Graded Non-convex Functions" by Doikov et al., 2024, and references there. For meta optimizer literature please see "MADA: Meta-Adaptive Optimizers through hyper-gradient Descent" by Ozkara et al. 2024 and the references there. For nonconvex optimization please see "Deterministic Nonsmooth Nonconvex Optimization" by Jordan et al, 2023. and minimization of majorization function please see Section 2 in Lectures on convex optimization by Nesterov, 2018.
2. The assumption 2 and standard Lipschitz continuous Hessian assumptions are not compared property. I think it is important to highlight the relation between Assumption on Lipschitzness of the hessian with constant $L_H$ and assumption 2. is it if and only if relation? how does $L_H$ from Hessian Lipschitzness correspond to $L_H$ from assumption 2?
3. On lines 234-237, it is said "We also note that our bound is on the rate at which the model’s performance increases (as measured by the loss function). This is in contrast to previous works, ...". I don't think it is true. Most of the results on nonconvex optimization (smooth) use bounds on a function decrease: $f(y) \leq f(x) + \langle \nabla f(x), x - y \rangle + \frac{L}{2}\|y - x\|^2$. By plugging $y=x_{k+1} = x_k - \frac{1}{L} \nabla f(x_k)$ and $x = x_k$ we obtain a bound on "the model's performance": $f(x_{k+1}) - f(x_k) \leq -\frac{1}{2L} \|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2$. 
4. Regarding results on lines 244-247, it seems that similar results can/was derived for second order smooth function. It is well known upper approximation of the function using second order information. The only difference, is that you use eigenvalue decompose of the hessian to provide this bound for all the eigenvectors directions, which in my opinion is not insightful. It would be beneficial to include more reference and comparison with a previous results on nonconvex optimization and the function's upperbounds. Can you please elaborate more on the contribution of this work in the context of existing literature on nonconvex optimization?
5. ELMO method does not define EIGEN function, which find $L_i$ for all i, which might be difficult to compute or estimate.
6. The convergence guaranties are not tractable from the classical optimization point of view and is not compared with previous results.
6. Numerical experiments does not provide enough details. Could you please provide these details, and also present wall-time plots?

Thank you for your valuable feedback. We wish to address some points raised to provide further clarification and insight into our work: 

***Regarding the Theoretical focus:***  
We agree that the paper leans toward the theoretical side, we leave extensive experimentation to future work.  We will make an effort to include further experiments applying AMOS to additional datasets, however experiments confirming other parts of the paper range across a variety of models and datasets, confirming the theory standing behind AMOS; see for instance section 5 and appendices J and L.   

Algorithm ELMO is developed primarily as a basis on which to build our algorithm quality metric while the paper’s focus is on optimizer selection; as a result, we leave experimentation on ELMO to future work to maintain focus on the optimizer selection problem.  We do present experiments validating the conclusions stemming from this metric (see section 5), including showing that the resultant meta-algorithm (AMOS) is beneficial to training in practice.   

While full Hessian eigendecomposition is difficult to apply to very large models such as LLaMa Behemoth, we can apply partial decomposition to smaller deep learning models (such as with Lanczos iterations); see e.g. [1], [2].  It is also possible to make simplifying assumptions about the Hessian, such as assuming diagonal structure, as is done in Adam and Sophia (which makes eigendecomposition trivial).  **We stress that AMOS does not add any overhead for Hessian computations, instead reusing the Hessians already computed by the second-order method given to AMOS; Concretely, in the experiments we use Sophia, which is a second order method.** Many second-order optimizers also compute some form of eigendecomposition of this Hessian ([1] and [2] perform Lanczos iterations while Sophia assumes diagonal structure), allowing us to reuse that as well.  In the paper, we provide 2 methods for computing Lipschitz parameters – one inspired by ARC’s Lipschitz parameter estimation approach (Appendix J.1) (in which we restrict ourselves to only a few eigenspaces using Lanczos iterations, a common theme in optimization, e.g. [1], [2]), and the other inspired by BFGS’s Hessian estimation approach (as in algorithm AMOS).  We acknowledge that these parameters may be computationally intensive to compute at every iteration, however we propose computing them periodically throughout training instead, following common practice for Hessian estimation (e.g. [1], [2], [3], [4]) and we demonstrate the value of this approach in our experiments.  This limitation is discussed in Appendix N, where we identify reducing the overhead of this subroutine as part of our planned future work, however we will further highlight this point in the final version of the paper.

summary.value: This paper proposes a new perspective on optimizer selection in machine learning by analyzing optimizer performance in relation to the local Lipschitz continuity of the Hessian in each eigenspace of a non-convex loss function. The authors develop ELMO, a minmax-optimal algorithm based on a refined cubic approximation, and show theoretically how descent rates can be tightly bounded even in regions of concavity. Building on this, they construct AMOS, a meta-algorithm that dynamically selects between first- and second-order optimizers based on per-parameter Hessian Lipschitz estimates, and empirically validate its performance—particularly on training language models with NanoGPT. The paper provides theoretical insights, a generalized optimizer regret bound, and empirical investigations of Hessian spectrum behavior during training.

strengths.value:
**1. Strong theoretical contribution**: The paper presents a careful derivation of descent rate bounds for quasi-Newton methods by leveraging a per-eigenspace Hessian Lipschitz continuity assumption.

**2. Empirical validation with strong visual results**: The experimental evaluation is comprehensive, covering from the CIFAR dataset to the modern transformer model nanogpt, supporting the paper’s main claims.

**3. Comprehensive Appendix coverage**: The appendices include substantial mathematical details, ablations, connections to prior metrics, and reproducibility details.

weaknesses.value: I am not an expert in optimization, from my perspective, the paper appears well-integrated. I will finalize my rating after reading other reviewers’ feedback and the authors’ rebuttal.

questions.value: **Q1.** Could the authors provide a comparison of time complexity across different methods? The current figures only report results in terms of iteration counts, which may be unfair to simpler algorithms that have lower per-iteration costs.

summary.value: This paper introduces a new optimizer, ELMO (Eigenspace-Lipschitz Minmax Optimizer), and a related meta-algorithm AMOS for dynamic optimizer selection. ELMO is derived from a theoretical analysis of loss function curvature using per-eigenspace Lipschitz constants, yielding a minmax-optimal update rule that generalizes quasi-Newton methods. Building on this theory, AMOS adaptively switches between first- and second-order optimizers (e.g., SGD and Sophia) during training based on estimated local curvature change rates.

strengths.value: The theoretical formulation is interesting and quite ambitious. The idea of analyzing optimizer behavior through eigenspace-specific Lipschitz parameters is novel and could deepen understanding of curvature-aware optimization. The distinction between convex and concave subspaces and the corresponding analysis of their Lipschitz distributions is also very interesting.

weaknesses.value: The work remains largely theoretical. ELMO itself is not evaluated experimentally, and the only empirical results are small-scale tests of AMOS on NanoGPT with the TinyShakespeare dataset, which again seems limited. The proposed approach is computationally heavy:computing or approximating per-eigenspace Lipschitz constants and Hessian eigendecompositions is not practical for modern large-scale models.

questions.value:
1. The experimental section does not clearly describe how the Hessian and parameter partitions are computed in practice. From the description, it seems you may use the Hessian estimator from Sophia and then aggregate per-tensor averages. Could you clarify the exact procedure? In particular, how is this implemented for block-diagonal Hessian structures?
2. In Figure 5, the final training loss appears to vary noticeably with different values of the hyperparameter​, which seems larger than the improvement shown in Figure 1 when comparing optimizers. Could you provide the exact final loss values for corresponding experiments in both Figure 1 and Figure 5?
3. Could you provide a wall-clock time comparison between AMOS and the baseline optimizers to illustrate the practical computational overhead of your approach?

summary.value:
Many reviewers find the ideas underlying the paper to be interesting; however, most also identify serious concerns and questions that remain unaddressed after the rebuttal period. These concerns span several aspects, including theoretical justification and convergence guarantees, the validity of the underlying assumptions, and the experimental design, particularly the breadth and depth of models and datasets considered. While the authors have attempted to address some of these issues, they explicitly defer several major concerns, such as broader experimental evaluations and deeper theoretical analysis, to future work.

Additionally, there are serious concerns regarding the computational demands of the proposed method, which relies on eigenvalue/eigenvector computations that may be prohibitively expensive and render the approach impractical for modern machine learning problems. Although the authors suggest various heuristics to mitigate these computational challenges, neither their practical effectiveness nor their theoretical implications have been demonstrated, and both require further investigation.

reviewer_concerns.value: Some concerns regarding the related work and the clarity of the presentation have been addressed. However, as noted above in the summary, many major concerns remain unresolved, particularly regarding the depth of the theoretical analysis, the motivation for and examination of the underlying assumptions, the adequacy of the experimental settings, and the computationally demanding nature of the proposed method.

reviewer_scores.value: Given that many concerns remain outstanding, I believe that the reviewers who raised significant issues and assigned low ratings would not have substantially revised their initial assessments.

***Regarding the ablations:***  

In Appendix K (line 1556), we demonstrate that equation 8 can be used to automatically select the Lipschitz threshold.  Since virtually all second-order methods estimate the Hessian only occasionally and the Lipschitz computations depend on the Hessian (such that we cannot compute Lipschitz parameters more frequently than the Hessian), we elect to compute the Lipschitz parameters at the same frequency as the Hessian estimations, since the Lipschitz computations do not add a significant amount of overhead beyond the existing Hessian computations (and so there is no need to estimate Lipschitz parameters less frequently than the Hessian). 

***We address the questions posed by the reviewers below:***  

1. The ambiguity would not raise any issues that we are aware of.  We eliminated the ambiguity merely as a matter of notational convenience in the proofs. 

2. AMOS is designd to combine first- and second-order methods; as a result, AMOS can rely on the Hessians already computed by the relevant second-order method, thus adding zero additional overhead for Hessian computations (this is the implementation used in our experiments).  As noted above, we will make an attempt to include wall-time experiments on the final version of the paper.  As far as memory constraints are concerned – AMOS requires storage for the Lipschitz parameters (one Lipschitz parameter for each of the n eigenvalues) and a copy of the n model weights (for computing the distance between consecutive model weight vectors), however the latter may be stored in low precision (since we only need the L2 norm of their difference, which is not significantly affected by precision change) and/or compressed with dimension-lowering techniques such as Fast Johnson-Lindenstrauss Transform [7], and both may be distributed among many machines with ZeRO [10], lowering the per-machine additional memory overhead inverse-proportionally to the number of devices with no additional communication overhead. 

3. All experiments were computed with Lipschitz parameters estimated from (naturally [8], [9]) noisy Hessian estimates.  For instance, Sophia uses the Gauss-Newton-Bartlett estimator, which is based on the square of (naturally) noisy gradients.  We leave further experimentation in this direction to future work.

***Regarding experiment details:***  
Due to spatial constraints, we were unable to provide full details on our experiments in the paper.  We refer the reader to details on our experiments (as well as further experiments) in Appendices J and K, and we will make an effort to include wall-time plots in the final version of the paper.  Given that AMOS adds computational overhead only to the occasional iterations in which the Hessian is estimated (and reduced overhead in all other iterations), and given that the additional complexity is relatively small (AMOS requires no eigendecomposition for Sophia and performs only O(n) additional flops (specifically: computing $|\theta_t – \theta_{t-1}|$ and $\lambda^i_t – \lambda^i_{t-1}$, dividing them, and updating the Lipschitz running averages), the wall-time is expected to be small.  In particular, distributed training systems suffer from a great deal of overhead per iteration (all-reduce gradient aggregation and all-gather gradient sharing communication overhead [10], [11], as well as time for saving checkpoints to NVMe [13] and time lost to node failures (which require a restart of the system from the last checkpoint) [12]), so that such systems draw particularly strong wall-time benefits from reduced iteration count, even in scenarios where single-device systems would see a wall-time increase.  Furthermore, in limited-data scenarios it is imperative to keep the iteration count low to avoid overfitting, and the same is true in streaming/online learning scenarios where each data point may only be used once before being discarded.

***We address the questions posed by the reviewers below:*** 
1. Although some previous work is broadly applicable to a wide range of optimizers (e.g. [3], [7]), most existing bounds (e.g. [4], [5], [6]) only apply to specific optimizers.  The result is that it is difficult to compare among optimizers using these bounds, since the assumptions and quality metrics vary significantly among different bounds. 

2. By “local concavity of parameter space”, we mean that there exists a ball of radius $\delta$ centered at position $x$ in the parameter space in which the function $f$ is concave (i.e. the Hessian is negative semi-definite).  We make use of eigendecomposition to decompose the parameter space into a pair of subspaces – one in which the loss function is locally concave (spanned by all the Hessian eigenvectors whose corresponding eigenvalues are non-positive) and the other spanning the remainder of the parameter space. 

3. “This” on line 138 referes to the Nonlinear Stepsize Control family studied by Garmanjani and Toint (see references in the paper on lines 137-138). 

4. Lines 151-154 discuss work by Amari etal., Bottou, and LeCun, who – under assumptions of a Hessian-faithful preconditioner and assuming we’re working in the convex “final phase” (discussed on lines 142-144) - prove that the variance of $\theta_t$ disappears at the limit, settling on $\theta^*$.  In effect, they define the convergence rate as the rate at which this variance disappears, and then provide a bound on this convergence rate. 

5. We introduce eigendecomposition (as detailed in our answer to question 2) to combat the problem of a Hessian matrix that is neither positive- nor negative- semi-definite.  Alain et al. and Ghorbani et al. (references in paper) discover experimentally that the eigenspaces corresponding to the negative eigenvalues of the Hessian (concave subspaces) contain a great deal of opportunity for descent, but this phenomenon is unexplained by most existing bounds (in which concavity does not imply an increased convergence rate) (e.g. [3]).  By contrast, our bound does agree with Alain and Ghorbani’s experimental results, since concave subspaces lower the bounds on $f(x_{k+1})$, implying more descent in concave subspaces. 

6. Answered above in the “Regarding the EIGEN function” paragraph. 

7. “Equal applicability” on line 269 refers to ELMO’s applicability to convex and concave subspaces.  This contrasts with many existing optimizers, which are only applicable to convex subspaces of the parameter space; see the introductory paragraph to section 2 (lines 174-178).  As an example, Saddle-Free Newton [2] applies Newton’s method in convex subspaces of the parameter space, but it simply applies Newton’s method with a modified version of the Hessian in concave subspaces, the Hessian matrix being modified by reversing the sign of all its negative eigenvalues.  However they fail to justify this approach mathematically, while we provide full mathematical justification for our approach to the concave subspaces, based on Lemma 3.1. 

8. Regarding computing the Lipschitz parameters, we provide two approaches – one inspired by ARC’s Lipschitz parameter estimation approach (Appendix J.1), and the other inspired by BFGS’s Hessian estimation approach (as in algorithm AMOS).  See our above paragraph titled “Regarding the EIGEN function”.

summary.value: The paper introduces ELMO, a per-eigenspace minimax optimizer derived from cubic upper and lower models of local loss decrease under eigenspace-wise Lipschitz smoothness assumptions. Additionally, the authors introduce AMOS, a meta-optimizer that dynamically switches between first- and second-order updates based on estimated curvature-change rates. The idea is to separate directions where the curvature varies slowly (favoring second-order updates) from those where it changes rapidly (favoring first-order). Experiments on TinyShakespeare with NanoGPT suggest AMOS (combining SGD and Sophia) can match or slightly outperform AdamW while saving compute.

strengths.value:
- S1: The paper introduces an original eigenspace-based formulation of curvature smoothness, replacing the usual global Hessian Lipschitz constant with per-direction Lipschitz parameters. This perspective is conceptually fresh and seems like it could influence future optimizer theory.
- S2: The derivation of the minimax ELMO step is mathematically clear and appears internally consistent. Its PSD quasi-Newton interpretation provides a robust theoretical link between cubic-regularization methods and practical quasi-Newton updates.
- S3: The presentation is generally clear, with well-structured definitions and pseudo-code for both ELMO and AMOS, the motivation for each design choice is also easy to follow.
- S4: AMOS demonstrates a practical direction for hybrid optimization: dynamically routing parameters between first- and second-order methods based on curvature-change estimates. In the small-scale tests provided it shows potential for compute-efficient optimization without loss of accuracy.

weaknesses.value:
- W1: The eigenspace Lipschitz assumption (and its estimation) is strong and not easily verifiable in practice.
- W2: Experiments are limited to a single small-scale setting, with no comparison to established second-order or hybrid baselines, it would be great to include e.g. K-FAC, Shampoo or cubic-regularization methods as a baseline.
- W3: The computational overhead and scalability are not quantified, making it unclear whether AMOS is viable for large models.
- W4: Experimental evaluation of ELMO is not included.
- W5: The paper is missing some important ablations on key hyperparameters such as the Lipschitz threshold and Hessian computation frequency.

questions.value:
- Q1: In Eq. (1), if the gradient happens to align with one eigenvector, all orthogonal directions have zero projection leaving their sign ambiguous. Does this ambiguity introduce any theoretical or practical issues from temporal inconsistencies?
- Q2: How often is the Hessian computed, and by what method (full vs. low-rank)? Please report the runtime and memory overhead relative to AdamW or Sophia.
- Q3: How stable is AMOS on larger or noisier settings e.g., with curvature estimated from stochastic gradients? Are there any observations on how noisy curvature estimates affect optimizer routing?

comment.value:
***We address the questions posed by the reviewers below:*** 

1. Sophia uses a diagonal estimator for their Hessian, and so eigendecomposition is trivial; at each (periodic) estimation of the Hessian we compute the Lipschitz parameters for each weight in the model using the BFGS-inspired method in AMOS (line 5 in algorithm AMOS), and then assign each tensor in the model the average of all its Lipschitz parameters.  For instance, for a model with 2 tensors, each of which is a 3-dimensional vector, we would compute the Hessian (which would have shape 6x6, of which we would store only the diagonal), then compute 6 Lipschitz parameters (one for each eigenvalue), then assign each of those 2 tensors the average of its corresponding Lipschitz parameters (i.e. the average of the first 3 Lipschitz parameters for the first tensor and the average of the last 3 Lipschitz parameters for the last tensor).  We will clarify this point in the final version of the paper.  In the block-diagonal case, after each Hessian evaluation (which would yield a block-diagonal Hessian), we would compute the eigendecomposition of each block (which would be computationally cheap for small blocks), then follow the same process with the resultant eigenvalues. 

2. While noting that AMOS may sometimes reduce training loss as a convenient side effect, that is not its primary goal; its primary goal remains improving training efficiency by integrating second-order optimizers only where relevant.  As such, figures 1 and 5 are only intended to demonstrate that using AMOS instead of pure Sophia retains similar training dynamics despite lesser application of Sophia, and not necessarily that the final loss will be lower with AMOS than otherwise.  While different momentum selections will lead to different training trajectories, figure 5 shows that these trajectories are relatively similar; we only trained our models for a relatively small number of iterations (2000 iterations) to demonstrate this effect.  The final loss value may be computed only after training the model to convergence. 

3. We will make an effort to include the results of wall-time experiments on the final version of the paper.  Given that AMOS adds computational overhead only to the occasional iterations in which the Hessian is estimated (and reduced overhead in all other iterations), and given that the additional complexity is relatively small (AMOS requires no eigendecomposition for Sophia and performs only O(n) additional flops (specifically: computing $|\theta_t – \theta_{t-1}|$ and $\lambda^i_t – \lambda^i_{t-1}$, dividing them, and updating the Lipschitz running averages), the wall-time is expected to be small.  In particular, distributed training systems suffer from a great deal of overhead per iteration (all-reduce gradient aggregation and all-gather gradient sharing communication overhead [5], [6], as well as time for saving checkpoints to NVMe [8] and time lost to node failures (which require a restart of the system from the last checkpoint) [7]), so that such systems draw particularly strong wall-time benefits from reduced iteration count, even in scenarios where single-device systems would see a wall-time increase.  Furthermore, in limited-data scenarios it is imperative to keep the iteration count low to avoid overfitting, and the same is true in streaming/online learning scenarios where each data point may only be used once before being discarded.

Thank you for your valuable feedback. We wish to address some points raised to provide further clarification and insight into our work: 

***Regarding the review and comparison to previous work:***  
Thank you for the helpful references, we’ll review them and add the relevant references to the final version of the paper, especially the review on meta-optimizers.  Due to spatial constraints we were unable to include the full related literature review in the paper, however see Appendices A and B in which we discuss related literature on nonconvex and preconditioned optimization.  Since most current training works with Adam or SGD we elected to compare against these in the paper, however we’ll also make an effort to include the results of additional experiments using alternative optimizers such as K-FAC and ARC in the final version of the paper in addition to Sophia and Adam. 

***Regarding comparison of the standard Hessian-Lipschitz assumption with Assumption 2:***  
We agree that assumption 2 is significantly more complex than the standard Lipschitz-Hessian assumption, however as we discuss in e.g. section 5, this additional subtlety is necessary for capturing the details of the loss function and does not significantly strengthen the standard assumptions (the $L_H$ from the standard assumption is roughly the same as the $L_H$ from assumption 2, with the exception that $L_H \geq L_R$ is an additional constraint on $L_H$ and $L_H$ from the standard assumption is required to be applicable to the entire parameter space while ours is only required to be applicable to the Hessians of parameter-vectors computed throughout training).  Due to the matrix L2 norm-spectral norm equivalence https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_norm#Spectral_norm, $L_H$ from the standard assumption is no less than the maximum of the per-eigenspace Lipschitz parameters).  In Theorem M.4 (see line 1881, Appendix M) we make a further comparison of assumption 2 with the standard Lipschitz-Hessian assumption.  We’ll highlight these comparisons in the final version of the paper to clarify the relation between the two assumptions. 

***Regarding the novelty of the function decrease bounds:***  
We agree that the lines in question are confusing to the reader, we’ve removed them in the revised rebuttal version. 

***Regarding our contribution to the nonconvex optimization literature:***  
The novelty of the observation on lines 244-247 is in introducing a new perspective to optimization on Lemma 3.1 – that of identifying its relevance to optimizers’ regret bounds.  This perspective is primarily intended as a necessary tool for understanding algorithm ELMO, rather than as a standalone breakthrough.  As shown in e.g. section 5, the eigendecomposition is important to expose the very significant variation among the Hessian Lipschitz parameters. 

***Regarding the EIGEN function:***  
In fact it is the LIPSCHITZ function, not the EIGEN function, that computes $L_i$ for each eigenspace.  The EIGEN function simply computes the eigendecomposition of the Hessian, which may be accomplished with Lanczos iterations, for instance.  Many second-order methods compute partial Hessian eigendecompositions unrelated to AMOS (e.g. [1], [2]) or use structure making eigendecomposition very easy (e.g. [9] uses diagonal Hessian structure), so that AMOS can simply reuse these eigendecompositions with no further overhead.  See footnote 2 (on line 373) for a discussion of methods of computing the LIPSCHITZ function; an additional example implementation of the LIPSCHITZ function is given in Appendix J.1 (in which we restrict ourselves to only a few eigenspaces using Lanczos iterations, a common theme in optimization, e.g. [1], [2]).  We acknowledge that these parameters may be computationally intensive to compute at every iteration, however we propose computing them periodically throughout training instead, following common practice for Hessian estimation (e.g. [1], [2], [8], [9]) and we demonstrate the value of this approach in our experiments.  This limitation is discussed in Appendix N, where we identify reducing the overhead of this subroutine as part of our planned future work, however we will further highlight this point in the final version of the paper. 

***Regarding the convergence guarantees:***  
Since the primary purpose of algorithm ELMO is to serve as a basis for our algorithm quality metric (which is used for our AMOS meta-optimizer), we leave an analysis of its convergence rate to future work.  However, we do note that ELMO is a special case of the ARC algorithm (thus automatically inheriting its convergence guarantees), and we compare the resulting quality metric against previous work in Appendix D.  Please note that AMOS does not concern itself with the absolute convergence rate or regret bound, instead focusing solely on the relative regret bound of a given algorithm compared against ELMO’s regret bound at each iteration. Also see Appendix C.
